metaTitle: Cash Conversion Cycle Calculator: See Your CCC in Days
metaDescription: Use this free cash conversion cycle calculator to track how long cash stays tied up in inventory and invoices before returning to your business.
introText:
A cash conversion cycle calculator measures how long operations tie up cash before customer sales return it to your bank account. In our default baseline, a business generates $1,000,000 in annual revenue alongside $600,000 in cost of goods sold (COGS). Carrying $90,000 in average inventory, $110,000 in accounts receivable, and $70,000 in accounts payable produces a cash conversion cycle (CCC) of 52.3 days.

That result reflects 54.8 days of inventory outstanding (DIO) plus 40.1 days of sales outstanding (DSO), minus 42.6 days of payables outstanding (DPO). At ModernWallet, we build financial tools to help business owners calculate the exact working capital gap their operations create. This gap shows whether cash reserves, a [business line of credit](/business-line-of-credit/), or [invoice factoring](/invoice-factoring/) best covers your ongoing overhead while waiting for collections.
howItWorks:
The cash conversion cycle formula traces how working capital moves through purchasing, customer billing, and supplier disbursements. The standard equation is CCC = Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) - Days Payable Outstanding (DPO). The formula adds the days your cash is locked in inventory and receivables, then subtracts the credit window your suppliers provide.

Days inventory outstanding measures the average number of days goods sit in storage before selling to customers. The formula is DIO = (Average Inventory / COGS) x Period Days. Dividing our default $90,000 inventory by $600,000 in COGS and multiplying by 365 days yields 54.8 days.

Days sales outstanding measures the average number of days your business takes to collect cash payments after completing a sale. The formula is DSO = (Average Accounts Receivable / Revenue) x Period Days. Dividing $110,000 in receivables by $1,000,000 in revenue and multiplying by 365 days yields 40.1 days of uncollected customer invoices.

Days payable outstanding measures the average number of days your company takes to pay suppliers for inventory and trade purchases. The formula is DPO = (Average Accounts Payable / COGS) x Period Days. Dividing $70,000 in payables by $600,000 in COGS and multiplying by 365 days yields 42.6 days of trade credit.

All calculations require figures from the exact same accounting period to produce accurate results. You can evaluate an entire year using 365 days, or examine an individual quarter by entering 90 days alongside quarterly financial statement numbers. Using an annual revenue figure with quarterly inventory balances distorts your cycle and produces misleading metrics.

A positive cash conversion cycle indicates the precise working capital gap your business must sustain between outgoing and incoming cash flows. In our 52.3-day example, your company must fund payroll, rent, and operating overhead for over seven weeks before sales revenue replenishes your account. Companies frequently bridge this timing gap by drawing on a revolving [business line of credit](/business-line-of-credit/) or by selling unpaid invoices through [invoice factoring](/invoice-factoring/).

When unexpected inventory purchases outpace established credit limits, some business owners turn toward a [merchant cash advance](/merchant-cash-advance/) to access rapid capital. However, evaluating your cash conversion cycle alongside your broader [operating cash flow](/operating-cash-flow/) indicates whether your operational margins can cover this timing gap organically. Generating strong operating cash flow allows your company to self-fund working capital needs instead of taking on recurring borrowing costs.

A negative cash conversion cycle occurs when days payable outstanding exceed the sum of inventory days and receivable days combined. If a merchant sells through inventory in 10 days and collects card receipts in 2 days while maintaining 45-day supplier payment terms, the resulting cycle is -33 days. That business collects cash from customers 33 days before paying its suppliers, so trade credit finances daily operations.

To see how operational adjustments release cash, consider the concrete impact of reducing collection times in our default baseline. If you shorten customer collection times by 10 days, DSO drops from 40.1 days to 30.1 days, reducing your total cycle from 52.3 days to 42.3 days. At $1,000,000 in annual revenue, each collection day represents roughly $2,740 in sales, so a 10-day DSO reduction releases over $27,000 in immediate cash into your bank account.

You can also reduce your cycle through better inventory turnover or extended supplier credit windows. Trimming slow-moving inventory reduces storage expenses and lowers DIO, while negotiating supplier terms from net-30 to net-45 increases DPO and preserves cash balances. Achieving small gains across all three operational levers compounds to release substantial liquidity and reduce reliance on outside debt.

faqs.question: What is the cash conversion cycle?
faqs.answer:
The cash conversion cycle measures the days between spending cash on inventory and collecting cash from customer sales, net of supplier payment terms. It evaluates operational efficiency across inventory management, customer billing, and trade credit terms. A lower cycle means working capital moves rapidly through your business, keeping liquidity available for payroll and operating overhead.

When this metric increases over consecutive quarters, cash is getting delayed in your daily operations. Unsold stock accumulating in warehouses or delinquent customer invoices are the standard causes of an expanding cycle. Monitoring this figure quarterly helps you spot working capital bottlenecks before they cause a severe cash crunch.

faqs.question: What is a negative cash conversion cycle and is it good?
faqs.answer:
A negative cash conversion cycle occurs when your days payable outstanding exceed the combined total of your inventory and collection days. In this scenario, your business collects cash from customer sales before you are required to pay your suppliers for that inventory. This setup is advantageous because suppliers effectively finance your everyday operations at zero interest.

Retail grocers and direct-to-consumer e-commerce brands frequently maintain negative cycles through rapid inventory turnover and instant card payments. However, operating with a negative cycle requires predictable sales demand and disciplined cash management. If customer sales drop unexpectedly, you must still pay your supplier invoices on schedule.

faqs.question: How do I lower my cash conversion cycle?
faqs.answer:
You lower your cash conversion cycle by reducing inventory holding periods, collecting customer receivables faster, or extending payment terms with your suppliers. Order stock in smaller batches and clear out slow-moving items with promotional pricing to lower days inventory outstanding. To accelerate customer collections, invoice immediately upon delivery, set firm credit terms, and offer early-payment discounts.

To increase days payable outstanding, negotiate with suppliers for 45-day or 60-day payment terms instead of standard 30-day windows. However, avoid delaying supplier payments if doing so forfeits early-payment discounts that exceed the interest rate of outside financing. Balancing all three levers keeps cash circulating through your operations rather than sitting idle on your balance sheet.

faqs.question: What is a good cash conversion cycle number?
faqs.answer:
A good cash conversion cycle depends on your industry, business model, and operational scale. No universal benchmark fits all companies. Service companies with zero physical inventory and immediate credit card billing often maintain cycles below 15 days. Conversely, equipment manufacturers that purchase raw materials and extend net-60 commercial credit routinely operate with cycles exceeding 90 days.

Rather than measuring your company against outside industry averages, compare your cycle against your own historical quarterly performance. A cycle that shortens over time demonstrates improving operational control and stronger liquidity. A steadily lengthening cycle indicates that cash is getting trapped in unsold inventory or overdue customer receivables.

faqs.question: How does the cash conversion cycle relate to needing a business loan or line of credit?
faqs.answer:
The cash conversion cycle reveals the exact calendar duration where your company must finance its operating costs before customer payments arrive. A 52-day cycle means you must cover payroll, facility leases, and utility bills for nearly two months before sales receipts replenish your accounts. That timing difference is the specific operational gap that short-term commercial financing is designed to bridge.

Knowing your cycle duration prevents you from guessing how much borrowing capacity your business actually requires. Companies with long inventory holding periods often draw on a revolving [business line of credit](/business-line-of-credit/) to purchase seasonal stock, while businesses facing delayed customer payments turn to [invoice factoring](/invoice-factoring/) to advance cash against open invoices. Before considering higher-cost borrowing options like a [merchant cash advance](/merchant-cash-advance/), check your [operating cash flow](/operating-cash-flow/) to confirm whether operational margins can bridge the gap sustainably.
